newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: World Bank sees Moldova loan once reforms go ahead.
newsitem.headline: World Bank sees Moldova loan once reforms go ahead.

text.p: The World Bank is ready to lend Moldova at least $60 million for structural adjustment as soon as the authorities decide to press on with promised reforms, an official said on Tuesday.

"We have developed a very detailed reform programme for Moldova, but political decisions are needed to implement it. The moment they are taken, the credit will be available," Hafez Ghanem of the World Bank told reporters.

But he said Moldova could follow Bulgaria's route to economic chaos unless decisions were taken soon. "Moldova's statistics look like Bulgaria's a year ago. It is very dangerous. The country is at a crossroad," he said.
Ghanem, who coordinates work on the World Bank's second adjustment loan to Moldova, has been meeting government officials to discuss moves Moldova must undertake to win the new loan.
The World Bank board is due to discuss the loan in July. The total sum of the loan is not determined yet, but it will be not less then the $60 million first adjustment loan.

James Parks, the World Bank's resident representative to Moldova, said the slow pace of structural reform was giving rise to concern about the Moldovan economy after an initial -- and successful -- period of stabilisation.
The former Soviet republic brought annual inflation down to 15.1 percent in 1996 and it has kept its leu currency stable and increased external reserves to $315 million.
But structural reforms have slowed, contributing to an eight percent GDP decline in 1996 and the build-up of payment arrears. Foreign debt skyrocketed to $1 billion, half of Moldovan GDP.

The new loan would aim to boost privatisation, strengthen the framework for public spending, reform the social safety net and the pension system and privatise the energy sector, which generates most of Moldova's foreign debt and internal arrears.
"Moldova's government realises that we can get out of the crisis only through speedy reforms, supported by international financial organisations," said Deputy Prime Minister Ion Gutu.
He said parliament and the government had 3-4 months to take unpopular decisions in energy, agricultural and social sectors.
"If we do not take these decisions, we would move along Bulgaria's road, and coming back would be much more painful," Gutu said.

The World Bank has approved a total of $231 million of loans to Moldova for seven projects to support private sector structural reforms, promote exports and develop the agricultural and energy sectors.
A three-year programme ending in 1998 provides annual disbursements of up to $100 million for the agricultural country of 4.3 million people between Ukraine and Romania.
